quotes.verbatim_quote:
This is an alternative approach to using octaves and is a softer but richer sound, which sounds very
authentic in the jazz guitar tradition.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the sonic rationale for choosing diads over octaves in solo jazz guitar arranging.

quotes.verbatim_quote: Place the root on beat 1 of each bar:
quotes.why_load_bearing: States the foundational rule for starting a walking bassline, anchoring all subsequent steps.

quotes.verbatim_quote: Now add either a diatonic or chromatic note on beat 4, above or below the following root note:
quotes.why_load_bearing: Introduces the approach-note concept on beat 4 as the second step in building a walking bass.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
To complete your walking bassline, you just need to add two more notes in between the root note of
beat 1, and the approach note of beat 4.

These can be any of the following:

e Diatonic notes from the scale of the given key.
e Chromatic notes, or
e Arpeggios.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Completes the four-step walking bass construction method by specifying the three note-type options for beats 2 and 3.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Now you can add shell voicings on the root notes on each bar.

It’s good to mix up playing them on the downbeat and on the ‘& of 1’ to create variety:
quotes.why_load_bearing: Explains how to layer chord voicings onto the walking bass and gives a rhythmic variation rule for keeping the texture fresh.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Notice how the walking bass is used to fill out sections where there is a long-held melody note — this
helps keep the drive and swing moving.
quotes.why_load_bearing: States the functional principle for when to deploy walking bass within a melody arrangement.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Option 1 (Diatonic Notes Only) Use Your Chord Dictionary

If you see extra notes you want to harmonize in the melody, and the notes are diatonic, you already
have what you need from this course.

Simply use voicings from the chord dictionary provided in Appendix 1 to harmonize the melody at
additional points.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the first passing-chord strategy and directs the student to the chord dictionary as the tool for diatonic harmonization.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
In this case, you can use a voicing on the note being approached, then play the same voicing one fret
away for the approach note in the melody:
quotes.why_load_bearing: Gives the mechanical rule for constructing a chromatic approach chord — same voicing shape moved one fret.

quotes.verbatim_quote: Tritone substitution is the process of substituting one chord for another a tritone away.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Provides the concise, definitional statement of tritone substitution.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
This is why a tritone interval is sometimes referred to as a split octave - as the tritone interval splits
an octave precisely in half:
quotes.why_load_bearing: Explains the symmetric interval property that makes tritone substitution work.

quotes.topic: guide tones swap in tritone sub
quotes.verbatim_quote:
C7 has E as the 3rd and Bb as the 7th.
F#7 has E as the 7th and A# (which is the same as Bb) as the 3rd.

The guide tones have essentially swapped places between these two chords.

Because the two chords have those 3rd and 7th as common tones, they can be substituted for
one another.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Explains the voice-leading mechanism — shared guide tones — that makes tritone substitution harmonically valid.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Tritone Substitution Rule - You can replace any chord with another whose root is a tritone
away from the root of the original chord.
quotes.why_load_bearing: States the practical application rule for tritone substitution in a single, memorable sentence.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
When it comes to solo guitar, you have the freedom to do these kinds of substitutions liberally as it’s
just you on stage.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Clarifies the performance context that permits free use of substitutions — solo setting vs. ensemble.

quotes.verbatim_quote: Rule: you can replace the I chord of a key with the vi chord of the key.
quotes.why_load_bearing: States the relative substitution rule in its most compact, actionable form.

quotes.verbatim_quote: Rule: you can substitute a major chord for chord iii of its key.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Provides the second major-to-minor substitution rule.

quotes.verbatim_quote: This process is referred to as chord addition — adding extra chords to the harmony.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Names and defines the technique of inserting substitution chords to expand the harmonic rhythm.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
You can use a minor 7 chord from the 5th of any dominant chord (which is like using the iim7 that
belongs to the dominant chord).

For example: an F7 chord’s 5th interval is C. So you could play Cm7 over F7 to get an interesting
sound.
quotes.why_load_bearing: States and illustrates the minor-for-dominant substitution rule with a concrete numerical example.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Joe Pass would often mention that the ii and the V chord can be interchanged with one another, and
this is the reason - they are very similar in their construction.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Cites the theoretical basis for the ii/V substitution by attributing it to Joe Pass.
